newsitem.title: UK: Olivetti puts brave face on tough times.
newsitem.headline: Olivetti puts brave face on tough times.

text.p: Management changes by information technology and telecommunications group Olivetti SpA were welcomed by analysts on Friday but they said the new team faced a tough job implementing a recovery plan for the struggling Italian company.
"It is good they changed the management...(but) it is a very difficult task ahead of them," said one analyst with an international bank who asked not to be identified.

Olivetti's new chief executive, Roberto Colaninno, appointed last month, came with executives Luciano La Noce and Corrado Ariaudo to explain to share analysts in London a plan outlined to the Milan market on Thursday.
Shares, which have been hammered in recent uncertainty, had opened higher in Milan after the meeting, touching 560 lire per share before easing back to close at 540 lire.

In London, executives fielded a range of questions on the plan, which calls for asset sales to raise 1.0 to 1.2 trillion lire ($660 to $790 million) in 1996 and 1997, including disposal of the personal computer business that put Olivetti on the world map.
Colaninno told the meeting that talks on the sale of the PC business were under way and it must be sold by the end of the year.

Executives said the company had the opportunity to earn operating profits by the end of the year and added that net debt should be cut to two trillion lire by then from 2.4 trillion lire at the end of August.
But sales which Olivetti had lost during recent instability, which has seen the resignation of chairman Carlo de Benedetti, who now has a non-executive role, would not be recovered.
"The overall feeling is that it's a good plan, superficially. But when you look more closely, all the things they need to achieve, it makes you wonder," the analyst said.

"There is very little margin for error," she added. Olivetti also plans to sell an eight percent stake in Omnitel Sistemi Radiocellulari to Germany's Mannesmann, which would still leave it with over 50 percent of the company and control.
Omnitel is a consortium led by Olivetti which owns a 70 percent controlling interest in Omnitel Pronto Italia, a fast-growing mobile phone business.
Where the mood in Milan had been reluctant over the Omnitel stake sale, analysts in London were more content. "I am not unhappy with the eight percent sale," the analyst said.
Olivetti will co-opt on to its board two new members in coming weeks to represent international investors, Colaninno told the London analysts.

Olivetti will be relying on its office equipment business, Lexikon, and its computer systems and services subsidiary -- both of which face declining profit margins -- to generate income in the years ahead, analysts said.

The fast-growing Omnitel, which has signed on 560,000 subscribers to its GSM digital mobile phone service in less than a year and now targets 700,000 by the end of the year, is not expected to turn a profit until 1998.
Analysts said the key question now was what Olivetti's international investors, who together hold 80 percent of the company, and its banks decide to do.
"I would be surprised if they pulled the plug," the analyst said but added that there were indications that a year-end deadline for signs of progress might be drawn.
"If the company does not meet the plan, where would the money come from?" to support it, she asked.
Shareholders would be unwilling to pay for another capital increase after a series of cash calls over recent years, analysts said, adding that banks were reluctant to extend further credit.
"The company is in a very critical situation," the analyst said. ($1=1520 Lire)
